transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-15 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Lopez (Redwood AE), Connor Blake (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood Solutions), James Park (Atlas Head of ML), Aisha Khan (Atlas Product), Liam O'Connor (Atlas DevOps)

Summary/Notes auto: quick orientation on prompt benchmarking lab, walk through of Console Evaluate/Compare, show regression alert demo, discuss pilot scope and security needs.

00:00 Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
00:04 James (Atlas): Yeah loud and clear, thanks Maya.
00:10 Maya: Quick context — we're gonna show the Redwood Console, the Optimize suggestions for batching/quant, and the Evaluate workspace where you can run prompt sets and A/B compare models. We'll keep it practical — show a small prompt set for product Q&A that Atlas mentioned in the intake form.
00:25 Aisha: Sounds good, main ask is we want an automated way to detect regressions after model swaps and a safe way to roll forward/rollback during canaries. Also interested in cost numbers.
00:40 Connor (SE): Great, we'll demo both alerting and the compare runbook. Also show the telemetry that ties per-prompt pass/fail to token cost and latency.
00:50 Liam (Atlas): FYI we've got a VPC requirement and customer-managed KMS for keys for PII, so any hosted sandbox should still respect that constraint.
01:00 Priya: Noted — we'll point to our Private options and the hybrid flows where you can run evaluation locally or in your VPC while control plane is in Redwood.

01:20 Maya: Ok jumping into the Console screen share — first page is the Evaluate dashboard, you can see prompt set groups, historical baselines, and a quick metric summary. (shared link: https://console.redwood.ai/atlas-demo — demo-only link)
01:40 Connor: I'll run a sample benchmark: 20 prompts in a "product_faq" set for Atlas. We're running two model variants — the hosted base and a quantized private variant — so you can see differences.
01:55 Speaker 1: (mumble) looks good.
02:10 Connor: Running now — note the streaming updates and per-example rows. For each prompt we capture generation, tokens, latency, a simple rubric that checks for factual correctness and hallucination flags. You'll see some imperfect transcriptions of model names in the grid, that's an artifact of the ingest pipeline.
02:40 James: When the rubric says "pass/fail" how customizable is that? We need multi-class for severity (minor, major, blocker).
02:55 Connor: You can define custom evaluators — regex checks, JS scoring functions, or human labels — and map them to severity. Alerts support thresholding by severity and aggregate drift detectors.
03:15 Aisha: Can those evaluators run in our environment so data doesn't leave our VPC?
03:25 Priya: Yes, we support private eval runners — the evaluation engine can be deployed in your VPC and post only aggregated metrics back to the Console, or use encrypted batched exports. We'll share the architecture doc.
03:45 Liam: Good, we need audit logs for who ran what and retention to satisfy internal audit.
03:55 Maya: We have audit logs, per-user traces, and you can forward them to your SIEM. We'll include sample syslog/CloudWatch configs in the security pack.

04:10 Connor: Back to the run — first few prompts show small diffs in phrasing but total token differences are 5-10 tokens per response for the quantized variant. See the cost column updating in real time — handy to quantify tradeoffs.
04:35 James: Can you annotate that column with projected per-100k cost?
04:40 Connor: Yep, the console supports cost-normalized metrics. We'll attach a CSV export so your finance folks can model run costs.

05:00 Connor: Now switching to A/B compare feature — you can create traffic splits, define holdback percentages, and pick evaluation buckets so certain prompts go to both models for direct comparison. This is how you get per-prompt lift/loss and statistically significant signals.
05:30 Maya: Important note — we do synchronous and asynchronous A/B. For low-latency endpoints you can do real-time traffic splits; for batch experiments you can run split replays on historical traffic.
05:45 Aisha: How do you avoid contamination? We can't have experimental content reach production users.
05:55 Connor: You can isolate experiments to a subset of users, use feature flags, or route only internal QA traffic. Also the conservative default is to mirror traffic to the variant and not expose it to users until you flip the rollout.
06:15 James: Show me an example regression alert — I want to see noisy vs actual regressions.
06:25 Connor: Sure, here's a synthetic regression we injected for demo: the model starts hallucinating a vendor name in the product description. The regression detector raises an alert when the fail-rate for a severity>major crosses 3% over baseline. Alert shows the failing examples, recent trend, and top contributing prompts.
06:45 Aisha: That's neat. What notification channels do you support?
06:50 Maya: Slack, PagerDuty, webhooks, and email. Slack messages include links back to the failing prompt and suggested rollback action in the runbook.
07:05 Liam: About rollback, can you automate a rollback policy? We need an automatic fallback when latency or error-rate crosses threshold.
07:15 Connor: Yes — rollouts are policy-driven. You can define automated rollback on latency, error, or quality regression. We also support phased rollouts with manual gate checks.
07:30 James: For the pilot we want a 2-model A/B with 10% holdback for 7 days and auto-rollback on quality regression. How do we tie this to success criteria?
07:45 Priya: We can define success criteria in the Evaluate project — e.g., median latency < 300ms, pass-rate uplift > 2% compared to baseline, cost delta < 15%. The Console will mark experiment success/fail and generate a summary PDF.
08:05 Aisha: If an alert fires, how easy is it for our PM to see the exact prompt examples where the model failed? We want to triage quickly.
08:15 Connor: Drill-down includes the original prompt, model outputs from both arms, scorer outputs, and editable notes. You can tag examples for human review and add them to a watchlist.

08:30 Maya: Switching briefly to Optimize suggestions — this is where Redwood gives recommendations for batching, KV cache lengths, and quantization level based on workload. For Atlas we recommended a mix: dynamic batching with a 50ms max latency, prefix-KV caching for repeat product queries, and int8 quant for the private variant.
08:55 James: Any idea of expected cost delta for the int8 quant?
09:00 Connor: Typically 20-35% on token compute for decode-heavy workloads; exact depends on sequence lengths. Our optimizer includes model-specific forecasts — we'll share the forecast CSV.
09:15 Aisha: And how do we trust the forecasts? We want guardrails so optimizer suggestions don't silently degrade quality.
09:25 Connor: Suggestions are advisory — you can stage them in a test cluster and run the Evaluate runner to compare before applying to production. We also surface quality regression risk scores with each suggestion.

09:45 Liam: Regarding the VPC/private deployment again — we need a network diagram for our infra team showing where the inference sits and what egress nodes are needed.
09:55 Priya: We'll include a VPC architecture diagram in the security pack. For fully air-gapped setups we also have an on-prem package but that adds lead time.
10:10 James: How long is lead time for Private with KMS integration?
10:16 Maya: Typical timeline is 4-6 weeks for the full on-prem or VPC private deployment with KMS integration; for hybrid/private control plane it's often 2-3 weeks. We'll propose timelines in the follow-up.
10:30 Speaker 2: (crosstalk)
10:45 Connor: Quick note about telemetry: we capture per-token latency, model-side errors, and an aggregation pipeline that can run locally. You can forward metrics to Datadog or BigQuery. We'll attach the telemetry schema.
11:10 Aisha: Do you do differential bias checks as part of regression? We care about hallucinations but also about fairness across customer segments.
11:20 Connor: You can include custom slice metrics and run per-cohort regression detection. The Evaluate tool supports cohort definitions and slice-level alerts.
11:35 James: Good. For the pilot dataset, we want to include at least 200 prompts drawn from our summit help center plus a smaller set of targeted edge-cases (payments, returns).
11:50 Maya: Perfect. For next steps let's capture that: we'll get the sample prompt spreadsheet from you, we'll spin up a sandbox project with two model variants (hosted + quant private), set up an A/B experiment with 10% holdback for 7 days, and enable regression alerts at severity>major 3% delta.
12:10 Aisha: Do you have a template for success criteria?
12:16 Priya: Yes — we'll send a starter success criteria doc with suggested KPIs.
12:25 Liam: Security questions — can you sign an NDA and start a short security questionnaire?
12:30 Maya: Absolutely, we've got an NDA + security pack ready, and we'll include SOC2 artifacts/links.

12:45 Connor: Demo wrap: I'll run one more fail-case playback so you can see how we group failures into triage tickets and tag owners. (plays sample)
13:05 James: I like how it highlights the delta lines.
13:12 Maya: Ok wrapping up — quick recap and next steps.
13:20 Maya (recap): 1) Atlas to share prompt set (200 prompts) and network constraints by Dec 18. 2) Redwood to provision sandbox project and send creds by Dec 16. 3) Redwood to send security pack (SOC2, KMS doc) and telemetry schema. 4) Schedule pilot check-in Dec 22.
13:45 Aisha: Sounds good. Any blockers we missed?
13:50 Liam: Nothing else from infra right now. We'll prioritize the network constraints doc.
13:55 Maya: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the links and the CSV exports.
14:05 Meeting ends.
notes: Demo focused on Console Evaluate and Optimize; customer emphasized VPC/KMS and audit logs. Pilot defined: 2-model A/B, 10% holdback, 7 days, auto-rollback on >3% major failures. Shared artifacts promised: sandbox link, telemetry schema, security pack, success-criteria template.
duration_alignment_comment: Transcript content roughly aligns to a 55 minute meeting — multiple demos and Q&A, plus recap and next steps.
